newsitem.title: PERU: World Bank set to sign Peru's Brady loan - paper.
newsitem.headline: World Bank set to sign Peru's Brady loan - paper.

text.p: The World Bank will approve on Thursday a $283 million loan for Peru, of which $233 million will go towards the start-up costs of the government's Brady Plan to restructure foreign commercial debt, leading financial daily Gestion reported Tuesday.

"Everything is ready. We are about to send the documents to the World Bank directors, who will consider it on the 19th of this month, on which date it will be approved," Gestion quoted World Bank representative in Peru Fred Levy as saying.
"In total, for the Brady plan, they will approve $233 million," he said, adding that the remaining $50 million would help fund imports. Officials at the World Bank in Lima and
the Peruvian Economy Ministry were not immediately available to confirm the report.
Levy told the newspaper the World Bank loan would be over 15 years at an annual interest rate of seven percent.

The Inter American Development Bank (IADB) also approved last month a $235.5 million loan to Peru as part of an $800 million financing package from the multilateral organizations to help fund the soon-to-be-completed Brady Plan.
The IADB loan followed a three-year, $358 million loan in July by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which was its contribution to the Brady financing package.
In November, the Peruvian government signed a Brady bond accord with its creditors containing the final details for the restructuring of $4.4 billion of principal and interest.
The formal closing of the accord was scheduled for mid- December, but now seems likely to be in early 1997.

In other comments in his interview with Gestion, Levy said that despite 1996's lower-than-expected economic growth, the Peruvian government had taken the "necessary corrections" to prevent what could have been a worse economic performance.
"I cannot criticize the results. I believe the necessary corrections were taken and and therefore we can anticipate a much better year in 1997," he said.
"If the government had not taken measures, and allowed inflation to rise or the current account deficit to become uncontrollable, the consequences would have been much more serious," he said.
After a deliberate government-led slowdown, economic growth for 1996 is now expected to be around 2.0 percent, down from 7.0 percent last year and 13.1 percent in 1994.

Although the government wanted to cool the economy, it was still hoping, however, for at least 3.0 percent growth this year. The January-October year-on-year Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rise was 1.7 percent.
"At a macroeconomic level, there are many factors that affect production levels which are beyond the government's control," Levy added.
